<doc title="Overview" path="guide/index.md">
# Overview

CoSky provides **configuration management** and **service discovery** for Spring Cloud microservices, using only **Redis** as infrastructure. There is no registry cluster to run: applications talk to Redis directly through the CoSky starters, and an optional REST API server adds a web dashboard, users and permissions.

## How it works

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#2d333b','primaryBorderColor':'#6d5dfc','primaryTextColor':'#e6edf3','lineColor':'#8b949e','secondaryColor':'#161b22','tertiaryColor':'#161b22'}}}%%
graph LR
    subgraph App["Each application"]
        style App fill:#161b22,stroke:#30363d,color:#e6edf3
        STARTER["CoSky starters"] --> CACHE["Local cache"]
    end
    subgraph Ops["Optional"]
        style Ops fill:#161b22,stroke:#30363d,color:#e6edf3
        SERVER["REST API server<br>+ dashboard"]
    end
    REDIS[("Redis")]
    STARTER -- "writes: Lua scripts" --> REDIS
    REDIS -- "changes: Pub/Sub" --> CACHE
    SERVER --> REDIS
    style STARTER fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style CACHE fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style SERVER fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style REDIS fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
```

- **Writes** (registering an instance, saving a config) are single Lua scripts, so they are atomic.
- **Reads** are served from a local cache in each application, so they cost no network round trip.
- **Changes** reach every cache through Redis Pub/Sub; a periodic resync covers messages lost while disconnected.

[Architecture](./architecture.md) explains the data model and the consistency guarantees in detail.

## Features

| Area | What you get |
|---|---|
| Configuration | Spring Cloud property source with live refresh, YAML / properties, versions with rollback, import and export (Nacos-compatible zip) |
| Service discovery | Spring Cloud `DiscoveryClient` and service registry, ephemeral instances with automatic expiry, metadata and status, weighted load balancing, service topology |
| Operations | REST API server with a web dashboard, JWT authentication, namespace-scoped roles, audit log, statistics |
| Isolation | Namespaces separate environments or tenants in one Redis |

## When CoSky fits

CoSky is a good fit when you already run Redis, use Spring Cloud, and want discovery and configuration without operating another cluster.

Consider an alternative when you need:

- **DNS-based discovery** or non-JVM clients without HTTP access to the REST API: CoSky clients are JVM libraries.
- **Health checks performed by the registry** (TCP/HTTP probes): CoSky instances prove liveness by renewing; a hung process that keeps renewing stays registered.
- **Strong consistency for reads**: application reads come from a local cache that is updated asynchronously (typically within milliseconds).

| | CoSky | Nacos | Consul | Eureka |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure | Redis | Nacos cluster + MySQL | Consul cluster | Eureka servers |
| Configuration | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (KV) | ❌ |
| Discovery | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Health check | Client renewal | Client beat, TCP/HTTP | TCP/HTTP/gRPC | Client beat |
| DNS interface | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Spring Cloud | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Where to go next

| I want to… | Read |
|---|---|
| Try CoSky in a Spring Boot app | [Getting Started](./getting-started.md) |
| Load and refresh configuration | [Configuration](./configuration.md) |
| Register and discover services | [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md) |
| Use CoSky without Spring | [Using the SDK](./sdk.md) |
| Run the REST API server and dashboard | [Deployment](./deployment.md), [Security](./security.md), [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) |
| Upgrade from 5.x | [Upgrading to 6.0](./upgrade-6.md) |
| Look up a property or an endpoint | [Configuration Properties](./properties.md), [REST API](./rest-api.md) |
| Understand the design | [Architecture](./architecture.md), [Performance](./performance.md) |
| Contribute | [Internals](./internals.md) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) |
</doc>

<doc title="Getting Started" path="guide/getting-started.md">
# Getting Started

In about ten minutes you will have a Spring Boot application that loads its configuration from CoSky, registers itself, and discovers other services, plus the dashboard to manage both.

**You need:** Java 17+, Docker (for Redis and the dashboard), and a Spring Boot 4 application built with Gradle or Maven.

## 1. Start Redis and the dashboard

```bash
docker network create cosky
docker run -d --name redis --network cosky -p 6379:6379 redis:7
docker run -d --name cosky --network cosky -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATA_REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379 \
  -e COSKY_SECURITY_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  ahoowang/cosky:6.0.0
```

The server creates the super user `cosky` with a random password on first start:

```bash
docker logs cosky | grep "init super user"
```

Open <http://localhost:8080> and sign in as `cosky`.

## 2. Add the dependencies

::: code-group

```kotlin [Gradle (Kotlin DSL)]
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-bom:6.0.0"))
    implementation(platform("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-dependencies:6.0.0"))
    implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-spring-cloud-starter-config")
    implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-spring-cloud-starter-discovery")
    // Loads bootstrap.yaml, where the CoSky config source is configured.
    implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-bootstrap")
    implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer")
}
```

```xml [Maven]
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>me.ahoo.cosky</groupId>
            <artifactId>cosky-bom</artifactId>
            <version>6.0.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>me.ahoo.cosky</groupId>
            <artifactId>cosky-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>6.0.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>me.ahoo.cosky</groupId>
        <artifactId>cosky-spring-cloud-starter-config</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>me.ahoo.cosky</groupId>
        <artifactId>cosky-spring-cloud-starter-discovery</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-bootstrap</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

:::

`cosky-bom` manages the versions of the CoSky modules, `cosky-dependencies` those of Spring Boot, Spring Cloud and the other libraries CoSky is tested with. Without `spring-cloud-starter-bootstrap` (or `spring.cloud.bootstrap.enabled=true`), `bootstrap.yaml` is ignored and no configuration is loaded from CoSky.

## 3. Configure the application

`src/main/resources/bootstrap.yaml`:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  data:
    redis:
      url: redis://localhost:6379
  cloud:
    cosky:
      namespace: dev
```

- The configuration loaded is `order-service.yaml` in the `dev` namespace (the application name plus `.yaml`).
- The application registers as service `order-service` on its web server port.

## 4. Create the configuration

In the dashboard:

1. Open **Namespace** and add `{dev}`. CoSky wraps every namespace in a Redis Cluster hash tag, so `dev` in the application is `{dev}` in Redis; applications do not add their namespace to this list themselves.
2. Open **Config**, select `{dev}`, and create `order-service.yaml`:

```yaml
greeting: Hello from CoSky
```

Read it like any Spring property:

```kotlin
@RestController
@RefreshScope
class GreetingController(@Value("\${greeting}") private val greeting: String) {
    @GetMapping("/greeting")
    fun greeting() = greeting
}
```

## 5. Run and verify

Start the application, then:

- `curl localhost:<port>/greeting` returns `Hello from CoSky`.
- Edit the config in the dashboard: the next request returns the new value, without a restart.
- **Service** in the dashboard lists `order-service` with one instance.
- Other applications reach it through Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, e.g. `http://order-service/greeting` with a `@LoadBalanced` `WebClient` or OpenFeign.

## Next steps

- [Configuration](./configuration.md): formats, refresh, versions and rollback.
- [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md): metadata, status, expiry and load balancing.
- [Deployment](./deployment.md): run the server in production.
- The [examples](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/main/examples) contain a provider and a Feign consumer.
</doc>

<doc title="Configuration" path="guide/configuration.md">
# Configuration

This guide is for application developers using the config starter, and for whoever manages configs in the dashboard. Setup is covered in [Getting Started](./getting-started.md).

## Which config an application loads

At startup the starter loads one config, identified by a **namespace** and a **config id**:

| | Property | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Namespace | `spring.cloud.cosky.namespace` | `cosky-{default}` |
| Config id | `spring.cloud.cosky.config.config-id` | `${spring.application.name}.${file-extension}` |
| Default extension | `spring.cloud.cosky.config.file-extension` | `yaml` |

These properties belong in `bootstrap.yaml`, and the application needs `spring-cloud-starter-bootstrap` (see [Getting Started](./getting-started.md#_2-add-the-dependencies)).

- **Format** follows the extension of the config id: `.yaml` / `.yml`, `.properties` or `.xml`. A config id without an extension uses `file-extension`.
- **Multi-document YAML** (`---`) is supported; a later document overrides an earlier one.
- **Precedence**: properties from CoSky override `application.yaml` and other local sources, as with any Spring Cloud bootstrap property source.
- **Missing config**: the application starts with a warning and no CoSky properties.
- **Redis unreachable**: loading waits up to `spring.cloud.cosky.config.timeout` (2s).

Several services can share settings by pointing `config-id` at the same config.

## Live refresh

When a config changes, every application using it receives the change through Redis Pub/Sub, typically within milliseconds, and the starter publishes Spring Cloud's `RefreshEvent`. What updates depends on how a value is read:

| How the value is read | Updated on change |
|---|---|
| `@ConfigurationProperties` beans | ✅ rebound |
| `@Value` in a `@RefreshScope` bean | ✅ the bean is recreated on next use |
| `@Value` in a regular singleton | ❌ keeps the startup value |
| `Environment.getProperty(...)` | ✅ |

The refresh event is published only after the local cache holds the new value, so a refreshed bean never reads the previous version. If an application misses a message (for example during a Redis reconnection), its cache resyncs within 5 minutes.

## Versions and rollback

Every save that changes the content creates a new version; saving identical content does nothing. CoSky keeps the **latest 10 versions** of each config and can roll back to any of them; rolling back saves the old content as a new version, so it can be undone too. A removed config can also be rolled back.

In the dashboard, **Config → History** lists versions with a diff against the current content. Through the API:

```bash
GET  /v1/namespaces/{namespace}/configs/{configId}/versions             # list versions
GET  /v1/namespaces/{namespace}/configs/{configId}/versions/{version}   # content of a version
PUT  /v1/namespaces/{namespace}/configs/{configId}/to/{targetVersion}   # roll back
```

## Import and export

- **Export** (`GET /v1/namespaces/{namespace}/configs/export`) downloads every config of a namespace as a zip, one file per config.
- **Import** (`POST /v1/namespaces/{namespace}/configs`, multipart field `importZip`) creates a config per file. `policy=skip` (default) keeps existing configs, `policy=overwrite` replaces them.
- **From Nacos**: a Nacos export zip imports as is. The `DEFAULT_GROUP/` prefix is dropped and other `/` become `-`.
- **Limits**: 10 MiB per zip, 64 MiB once unzipped. Directories and hidden files are skipped.

## Turning it off

`spring.cloud.cosky.config.enabled=false` disables the config starter; `spring.cloud.cosky.enabled=false` disables CoSky entirely.

## See also

- [Configuration Properties](./properties.md) for every property.
- [Using the SDK](./sdk.md#configuration) to read and watch configs without Spring.
- [Architecture](./architecture.md#consistency-model) for how the cache stays consistent.
</doc>

<doc title="Service Discovery" path="guide/service-discovery.md">
# Service Discovery

This guide is for application developers using the discovery starter. Setup is covered in [Getting Started](./getting-started.md).

## Registration

With the discovery starter on the classpath, an application registers itself once its web server has started, and deregisters on graceful shutdown. Its instance is described by:

| Field | Property (`spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.registry.*`) | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Service id | `service-id` | `spring.application.name` |
| Host | `host` | first non-loopback IP address |
| Port | `port` | the web server port |
| Scheme | `schema` | `http` |
| Weight | `weight` | `1` |
| Metadata | `metadata.<key>` | none |
| Status | `initial-status` | `UP` (stored as metadata `instance_status`) |

The instance id is `<serviceId>@<scheme>#<host>#<port>`, so an instance re-registering from the same address replaces itself.

`spring.cloud.service-registry.auto-registration.enabled=false` keeps an application discoverable-only: it discovers others without registering.

## Staying registered: ephemeral instances

By default an instance is **ephemeral**: it lives for a TTL and must keep renewing it.

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#2d333b','primaryBorderColor':'#6d5dfc','primaryTextColor':'#e6edf3','lineColor':'#8b949e','secondaryColor':'#161b22','tertiaryColor':'#161b22'}}}%%
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Registered: register
    Registered --> Registered: renew every 10s (TTL 60s)
    Registered --> [*]: deregister on shutdown
    Registered --> Expired: no renewal for 60s
    Expired --> [*]: removed, "expired" event
    Expired --> Registered: renewal finds it gone and registers again
```

- `renew.period` (10s) must stay well below `ttl` (60s), so that a few missed renewals do not expire a healthy instance.
- An expired instance is removed and announced by any registered CoSky client in the namespace; no server needs to run.
- If an instance expired anyway, for example during a network partition, its next renewal registers it again with the metadata set since it first registered.
- Consumers never receive an instance whose TTL has passed, even before it is removed.

**Fixed instances** (`is-ephemeral: false`) never expire and are not renewed. Use them for endpoints that cannot run the client, such as a database proxy registered through the [REST API](./rest-api.md); remove them explicitly.

Liveness is proven by renewing only: CoSky does not probe instances. A process that hangs but keeps its renewal thread alive stays registered; combine CoSky with health-aware routing or circuit breakers where that matters.

## Discovering services

Applications discover through Spring Cloud's standard APIs, backed by a local cache that change events keep current:

```kotlin
@Autowired lateinit var discoveryClient: DiscoveryClient          // or ReactiveDiscoveryClient

discoveryClient.services                                          // service ids in the namespace
discoveryClient.getInstances("order-service")                     // live instances
```

With `spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer`, `@LoadBalanced` `WebClient` / `RestClient` and OpenFeign resolve `http://order-service/...` through CoSky.

Discovery is scoped to the application's namespace. Lookups are answered from memory; the first lookup of a service loads it from Redis and subscribes to its changes.

## Metadata and status

Metadata is a string map attached to an instance, e.g. a zone or a version. Set it at registration with `registry.metadata.*`, edit it in the dashboard, or at runtime through the [SDK](./sdk.md#service-discovery).

Spring Cloud's `ServiceRegistry.setStatus` (for example through the `/actuator/serviceregistry` endpoint) stores the status as the `instance_status` metadata.

Spring Cloud discovery returns only instances whose status is `UP`, or that have no status (such as fixed instances registered through the REST API). Setting an instance to `OUT_OF_SERVICE` therefore takes it out of rotation without deregistering it, and setting it back to `UP` returns it. Set `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.filter-only-up-instances=false` to receive every instance.

## Load balancing and weights

| Client | Algorithm | Uses weights |
|---|---|---|
| Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (default) | Round robin | ❌ |
| Spring Cloud LoadBalancer with `spring.cloud.loadbalancer.configurations=weighted` | Weighted | ✅ |
| CoSky `LoadBalancer` bean (`BinaryWeightRandomLoadBalancer`) | Weighted random | ✅ |

CoSky exposes each instance's weight as the `weight` metadata of Spring Cloud instances, which is where Spring Cloud LoadBalancer's weighted configuration reads it. Code using the CoSky API directly can inject CoSky's `LoadBalancer` and call `choose(namespace, serviceId)`. The SDK also provides `RandomLoadBalancer` (ignores weights) and the `ArrayWeightRandomLoadBalancer` / `TreeWeightRandomLoadBalancer` variants, which choose by weight like the default with different memory and lookup trade-offs.

## Service topology

Each application records itself as a consumer of the services it discovers, and the dashboard draws the resulting dependency graph. Turn it off with `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.topology-enabled=false`. A discovered service from another namespace appears as `<namespace>.<serviceId>`.

## See also

- [Configuration Properties](./properties.md#service-discovery) for every property.
- [Using the SDK](./sdk.md#service-discovery) to register and discover without Spring.
- [Architecture](./architecture.md#service-discovery) for the data model and expiry mechanics.
</doc>

<doc title="Using the SDK" path="guide/sdk.md">
# Using the SDK

The Spring Cloud starters wire everything for you. Use the SDK directly when you are not on Spring Cloud, or need finer control: managing configs from a tool, registering an instance on behalf of another process, or watching a config.

All APIs are reactive (Project Reactor `Mono` / `Flux`) and take the namespace explicitly. Namespaces must not be blank or contain `:`; wrap them in a hash tag (e.g. `{dev}`) when Redis runs in cluster mode.

## Dependencies

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-bom:6.0.0"))
    implementation(platform("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-dependencies:6.0.0"))
    implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-config")     // configuration
    implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-discovery")  // service discovery
}
```

Both build on Spring Data Redis with Lettuce:

```kotlin
val connectionFactory = LettuceConnectionFactory("localhost", 6379).apply { afterPropertiesSet() }
val redisTemplate = ReactiveStringRedisTemplate(connectionFactory)
// Shared by every cache that follows changes.
val listenerContainer = ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer(connectionFactory)
```

## Configuration

`RedisConfigService` reads and writes Redis directly; `RedisConsistencyConfigService` adds the local cache kept current by change events, and is what applications should read through.

```kotlin
val redisConfigService = RedisConfigService(redisTemplate)
val configService = RedisConsistencyConfigService(
    delegate = redisConfigService,
    configEventListenerContainer = RedisConfigEventListenerContainer(listenerContainer),
)

configService.setConfig("{dev}", "order-service.yaml", "greeting: hello").block()
configService.getConfig("{dev}", "order-service.yaml").block()?.data      // served from memory after the first read

// The current snapshot, then one snapshot per change, after the cache is updated.
configService.watchConfig("{dev}", "order-service.yaml")
    .subscribe { snapshot -> println("v${snapshot.version}: ${snapshot.value?.data}") }

configService.getConfigVersions("{dev}", "order-service.yaml").collectList().block()
configService.rollback("{dev}", "order-service.yaml", targetVersion = 1).block()

configService.close()   // stops listening when you are done
```

## Service discovery

### Registering and renewing

```kotlin
val registry = RedisServiceRegistry(RegistryProperties(instanceTtl = Duration.ofSeconds(60)), redisTemplate)
val renewal = RenewInstanceService(RenewProperties(period = Duration.ofSeconds(10)), registry)

val instance = Instance.asInstance(serviceId = "order-service", schema = "http", host = "10.0.0.5", port = 8080)
    .asServiceInstance(weight = 2, metadata = mapOf("zone" to "a"))

registry.register("{dev}", instance).block()
renewal.start()        // renews every registered ephemeral instance and reaps expired ones

registry.setMetadata("{dev}", instance.serviceId, instance.instanceId, "zone", "b").block()   // one key
registry.setMetadata("{dev}", instance.serviceId, instance.instanceId, mapOf("zone" to "b")).block() // replace all

renewal.stop()
registry.deregister("{dev}", instance).block()
```

Register a fixed instance with `asServiceInstance(isEphemeral = false)`; it is never renewed nor expired.

### Discovering

```kotlin
val discovery = ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscovery(
    delegate = RedisServiceDiscovery(redisTemplate),
    serviceEventListenerContainer = RedisServiceEventListenerContainer(listenerContainer),
    instanceEventListenerContainer = RedisInstanceEventListenerContainer(listenerContainer),
)

discovery.getServices("{dev}").block()                       // List<String>
discovery.getInstances("{dev}", "order-service").block()     // List<ServiceInstance>, expired ones excluded

val loadBalancer = BinaryWeightRandomLoadBalancer(discovery)
loadBalancer.choose("{dev}", "order-service").block()        // weighted random choice

discovery.close()
```

Each call returns an immutable snapshot; an unchanged snapshot is the same list instance, so caching derived data per snapshot is cheap.

## See also

- [Architecture](./architecture.md) for the data model, events and consistency guarantees.
- The tests under `cosky-config` and `cosky-discovery` exercise every API against Redis.
</doc>

<doc title="Deployment" path="guide/deployment.md">
# Deployment

This page is for operators running the **REST API server**, which serves the REST API and the dashboard. Applications using the starters do not need it: they only need Redis.

The server is stateless; all state lives in Redis. Run as many instances as you need behind a load balancer, with the **same JWT secret** on each.

## Before you start

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| Redis reachable from the server | All data lives there. See [Preparing Redis](#preparing-redis). |
| A JWT secret (`COSKY_SECURITY_KEY`), random, ≥ 32 characters | The server refuses to start without one while security is enabled. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 32`. |
| Port 8080 | REST API and dashboard. |

## Docker

Images are published for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` to `ahoowang/cosky`, `ghcr.io/ahoo-wang/cosky` and `registry.cn-shanghai.aliyuncs.com/ahoo/cosky`, tagged `6.0.0` and `6.0`.

```bash
docker run -d --name cosky -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATA_REDIS_URL=redis://redis.example.com:6379 \
  -e COSKY_SECURITY_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  ahoowang/cosky:6.0.0
```

A Compose file starting Redis with persistence and CoSky:

```yaml
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
  cosky:
    image: ahoowang/cosky:6.0.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      COSKY_SECURITY_KEY: ${COSKY_SECURITY_KEY:?set COSKY_SECURITY_KEY to a random secret}
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
volumes:
  redis-data:
```

The image runs as a non-root user and defines a health check on `/actuator/health`.

## Kubernetes

The repository provides manifests in [`k8s/deployment`](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/main/k8s/deployment): `cosky.yml` for a standalone Redis, `cosky-cluster.yml` for Redis Cluster, and `cosky-service.yaml` exposing port 80.

```bash
kubectl create secret generic cosky-secret --from-literal=security-key="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
kubectl create secret generic redis-secret \
  --from-literal=host=redis.default.svc --from-literal=password='<redis password>'
# for Redis Cluster: --from-literal=nodes=node1:6379,node2:6379,node3:6379 instead of host
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment/cosky.yml -f k8s/deployment/cosky-service.yaml
```

- Startup, readiness and liveness probes use `/actuator/health`, `/actuator/health/readiness` and `/actuator/health/liveness`.
- Requests are 250m CPU / 1 GiB memory, limits 1 CPU / 1.25 GiB; the JVM heap is fixed at 512 MiB (see [JVM options](#jvm-options)).
- The pod is annotated for the OpenTelemetry Operator's Java auto-instrumentation; remove the annotation if you do not run the operator.

## Standalone distribution

Build the distribution from source (JDK 17+, and Node.js 22.12+ with pnpm for the dashboard):

```bash
cd dashboard && pnpm install && pnpm build && cd ..   # without this, the server has no web UI
./gradlew :cosky-rest-api:distTar
tar -xvf cosky-rest-api/build/distributions/cosky-rest-api-6.0.0.tar
cd cosky-rest-api-6.0.0
COSKY_SECURITY_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" bin/cosky-rest-api \
  --spring.data.redis.url=redis://localhost:6379
```

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| `bin/cosky-rest-api` | Start script; extra JVM options go in `JAVA_OPTS` |
| `config/application.yaml`, `config/bootstrap.yaml` | Configuration, read instead of the defaults bundled in the jar |
| `ui/` | Dashboard |
| `logs/` | Application log (`cosky-rest-api.log`) and GC logs |
| `data/` | Heap dumps on `OutOfMemoryError` |

Run the script from the distribution directory: it resolves `config/`, `logs/` and `data/` relative to the working directory.

### JVM options

The start script (and the Docker image) runs with a fixed 512 MiB heap, ZGC, GC logging to `logs/` and heap dumps to `data/`. Add options through `JAVA_OPTS`, for example a larger heap (`-Xmx1g`), or remote JMX with authentication and TLS when you need it.

## Configuring the server

Any property can be set as an environment variable (`SPRING_DATA_REDIS_URL`), a command-line argument (`--spring.data.redis.url=…`) or in `config/application.yaml`. The ones operators usually set:

| Environment variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `SPRING_DATA_REDIS_URL` | `redis://localhost:6379` | Redis connection; or `SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST`, `_PORT`, `_PASSWORD` |
| `SPRING_DATA_REDIS_CLUSTER_NODES` | — | Redis Cluster nodes, comma-separated |
| `COSKY_SECURITY_KEY` | — (required) | JWT signing secret |
| `COSKY_SUPER_INIT` | `false` | `true` resets the super user's password at every start; set it once to recover access, then remove it |
| `COSKY_NAMESPACE` | `cosky-{system}` | Namespace of the server's own config and registration |
| `COSKY_AUTO_REGISTRY` | `true` | Register the server itself as service `cosky-rest-api` |
| `SERVER_PORT` | `8080` | HTTP port |

The full list is in [Configuration Properties](./properties.md#rest-api-server).

### First start

On first start the server creates the super user `cosky` with a random password and prints it to the log:

```bash
docker logs cosky | grep "init super user"        # or: grep "init super user" logs/cosky-rest-api.log
```

Sign in at `http://<server>:8080`, then create users and roles: see [Security](./security.md).

## Preparing Redis

| Concern | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Version and mode | Any maintained Redis release, standalone, Sentinel or Cluster. No modules or Redis Functions are needed. |
| Persistence | Enable AOF (`appendonly yes`) or RDB snapshots: configs, users and roles exist only in Redis. Instances are re-registered by their renewals after a restart. |
| Eviction | Use `maxmemory-policy noeviction`, or keep CoSky in a Redis without `maxmemory`: an evicted key is a lost config or instance. |
| Cluster | Every key of a namespace carries the namespace's hash tag (the starters add `{…}` automatically), so a namespace lives in one slot and Lua scripts stay valid. |
| Security | Require a password (`requirepass` or ACLs) and keep Redis on a private network; anyone who can write to it can change configs and registrations. |

## Upgrading

Upgrade servers one at a time; the key schema is shared across versions. Read [Upgrading to 6.0](./upgrade-6.md) when coming from 5.x.
</doc>

<doc title="Security" path="guide/security.md">
# Security

This page is for administrators of the REST API server. Security covers the server's API and dashboard; applications using the starters access Redis directly, so protect Redis itself (see [Deployment](./deployment.md#preparing-redis)).

## Model

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Super user** `cosky` | Created on first start; can do everything and can be neither locked nor removed. |
| **User** | Signs in with a password (stored as a BCrypt hash, at most 72 bytes) and holds roles. |
| **Role** | Grants `r` (read), `w` (write) or `rw` (both) on namespaces. The built-in `admin` role grants everything, including user and role management. |
| **Policy** | Rules evaluated before roles: public endpoints, what any signed-in user may do, and the `admin` / super user grants. |

A request is allowed when the policy allows it; otherwise when one of the user's roles grants the action on the namespace in the request path (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE` need `r` or `rw`; `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` need `w` or `rw`).

Signed-in users without roles can only list the namespaces their roles grant (`GET /v1/namespaces`, so an empty list) and read the server's own namespace name.

## Common tasks

All of these are available in the dashboard (**User**, **Role**) and through the [REST API](./rest-api.md#users-roles-and-audit).

**Give a team read access to a namespace**

1. Create a role, e.g. `payments-read`, with `{prod}` → `r`.
2. Create the users and bind them to the role.

A user bound to several roles gets the union of their grants. A removed role grants nothing but stays bound to its users until they are rebound.

**Make someone an administrator**: bind the `admin` role.

**Lock a user out**: lock the user; sign-in and token refresh are rejected until the user is unlocked.

**Recover the super user**: start the server once with `COSKY_SUPER_INIT=true` (`cosky.security.enforce-init-super-user`), read the new password from the log, then remove the variable; while it is set, the password is reset at every start.

## Tokens

Signing in returns a JWT access token (valid 15 minutes) and a refresh token (valid 3 hours), signed with `cosky.security.key`. Clients send `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` and exchange the refresh token for a new pair before it expires.

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `cosky.security.key` (`COSKY_SECURITY_KEY`) | none: the server refuses to start without it |
| `cosec.jwt.token-validity.access` | `15m` |
| `cosec.jwt.token-validity.refresh` | `3H` |

Changing the key invalidates every issued token, which signs everybody out. Use the same key on every server instance.

## Failed sign-ins

After 10 failed attempts a user is locked out, and the lock lifts 15 minutes after the last attempt. The user list shows who is locked; an administrator can unlock earlier.

## Customizing the policy

The bundled policy allows without sign-in: `OPTIONS` requests, the dashboard's static files, Swagger UI, `/actuator/health`, and sign-in / token refresh. It allows any signed-in user to call `GET /v1/namespaces` and `GET /v1/namespaces/current`, and grants everything to the `admin` role and to `cosky`.

To change it, save a [CoSec policy](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSec) as the config `cosky-policy.json` in the `cosky-{system}` namespace, starting from the [bundled one](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/cosky-rest-api/src/main/resources/cosky-policy.json). Every server instance applies it as soon as it is saved; a policy that does not parse is rejected with an error in the log and the previous one stays in force.

## Audit log

The server records each request it handles: operator, IP, path, method, status, error message and time. By default only write operations are recorded.

| Setting | Default | Values |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.security.audit-log.action` | `write` | `read`, `write`, `rw` |
| `cosky.security.audit-log.max-size` | `100000` | newest entries kept |

The dashboard's **Audit Log** filters by text, time range and outcome, and exports CSV.

## Turning security off

`cosky.security.enabled=false` disables authentication and authorization altogether. Only do this when the server is reachable exclusively by trusted clients.
</doc>

<doc title="Dashboard" path="guide/dashboard.md">
# Dashboard

The REST API server serves a web dashboard at `http://<server>:8080`. Sign in with a CoSky user (see [Security](./security.md)); each page works on the namespace selected at the top, and only shows what your roles grant.

| Page | What you do there |
|---|---|
| **Home** | Counts of namespaces, configs, services and instances, and the service topology |
| **Config** | Create, edit and remove configs; browse the history with diffs and roll back; import and export zips |
| **Service** | Browse services and instances, register fixed instances, edit metadata, deregister |
| **Namespace** | Add and remove namespaces |
| **User** | Create users, bind roles, lock, unlock, change passwords |
| **Role** | Define roles and the namespaces they grant |
| **Audit Log** | Search who did what, filter by time and outcome, export CSV |

![Home](/dashboard-dashboard.png)

## Configs

![Configs](/dashboard-config.png)

Saving a config creates a new version that every application using it receives within milliseconds. The history compares any version with the current one and rolls back to it; see [Configuration](./configuration.md#versions-and-rollback).

![Rollback](/dashboard-config-rollback.png)

## Services

![Services](/dashboard-service.png)

Instances registered by applications appear and disappear on their own. Fixed instances added here stay until removed; see [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md).

![Topology](/dashboard-topology.png)

## Users, roles and audit

![Roles](/dashboard-role.png)

![Audit log](/dashboard-audit-log.png)

## Developing the dashboard

The dashboard is a React application in [`dashboard/`](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/main/dashboard); its README describes the development server, tests and the API client generation.
</doc>

<doc title="Upgrading to 6.0" path="guide/upgrade-6.md">
# Upgrading to 6.0

CoSky 6.0 rebuilds the consistency layer, hardens security and bounds the data kept in Redis. The Redis key schema is unchanged, so 5.x and 6.0 clients can share a namespace during a rolling upgrade.

## Recommended order

1. **Upgrade the REST API servers** — set a JWT secret first (see below), then roll out 6.0.
2. **Grant namespace roles** to users who are not admins, and update a stored policy if you have one.
3. **Upgrade the applications** using the starters or the SDK, fixing the API changes below.
4. **Once every client runs 6.0**, optionally enable `renew-event-carries-ttl-at`.

## REST API server

### A JWT secret is required

With security enabled (the default), the server refuses to start unless `cosky.security.key` is set. Tokens used to be signed with a secret published in the repository.

```bash
export COSKY_SECURITY_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
```

Use the same secret on every server instance. Changing it invalidates all issued tokens. The Docker, Kubernetes and standalone examples in this wiki already pass `COSKY_SECURITY_KEY`.

### Users need roles to read namespaces

The default policy used to let every authenticated user read every namespace. It now only grants `GET /v1/namespaces` (which lists the namespaces the user's roles cover) and `GET /v1/namespaces/current`; everything else needs a role. Give each non-admin user a role with read (`r`) or read-write (`rw`) access to the namespaces they work with — see [Security](./security.md).

If you stored your own policy (config `cosky-policy.json` in the `cosky-{system}` namespace), it overrides the bundled one: replace the `namespace` statement's pattern `/v1/namespaces/**` with `["/v1/namespaces", "/v1/namespaces/current"]`.

### Other server changes

| Change | What to do |
|---|---|
| Passwords are hashed with BCrypt | Nothing: existing hashes keep working and are upgraded on each user's next login. New passwords are limited to 72 bytes. |
| `PUT /v1/namespaces/current/{namespace}` removed | It switched the namespace of the whole server for every user. Pass the namespace in each request path instead. |
| Config history keeps the latest 10 versions | Older versions are trimmed on the next change of each config. |
| The audit log keeps the newest 100,000 entries | Tune with `cosky.security.audit-log.max-size`. |
| Config imports are limited | Zip files up to 10 MiB, 64 MiB once unzipped. |

## Applications (starters and SDK)

### Configuration

- `spring.cloud.cosky.enabled=false` now disables discovery and registration too.
- New: `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.topology-enabled` (default `true`) controls whether the application records itself as a consumer of the services it discovers.
- `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.registry.is-ephemeral` still binds.

### API changes

These only affect code that uses the CoSky classes directly, not applications that use Spring Cloud's `DiscoveryClient` or `@Value`/`@ConfigurationProperties`.

| 5.x | 6.0 |
|---|---|
| `ServiceDiscovery.getServices(namespace)` / `getInstances(namespace, serviceId)` return `Flux` | They return `Mono<List<…>>` snapshots. An unchanged snapshot is the same list instance. |
| Overloads without a namespace, `NamespacedContext`, `ServiceInstanceContext` | Removed: pass the namespace explicitly. A namespace must not be blank or contain `:`. |
| `EventListenerContainer` is `AutoCloseable` with `receive(topic)` | `listen(topic)` emits the event stream once the subscription is active; `receive(topic)` remains. |
| Load balancers take a `ServiceDiscovery` and an `InstanceEventListenerContainer` | They take only the `ServiceDiscovery`, e.g. `RandomLoadBalancer(serviceDiscovery)`. |
| Reset hooks on the consistency services | Removed: watch changes with `ConfigWatcher.watchConfig(namespace, configId)`. |
| `RedisServiceTopology(redisTemplate)` | `RedisServiceTopology(redisTemplate, consumer)`, where `consumer` is the local `NamespacedServiceId`. |
| `ServiceRegistry.setMetadata(…, key, value)` replaced all metadata | It now sets that key only; `setMetadata(…, map)` still replaces all metadata. |
| `ServiceInstance` equality compares the address (instance id, schema, host, port) | Equality is structural: weight, ephemeral, ttlAt and metadata count too. |

## Mixed versions

- Instances registered by 5.x clients keep being cleaned up when they expire. 6.0 clients also index ephemeral instances by expiry, so `expired` events no longer depend on the REST API server.
- `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.registry.renew-event-carries-ttl-at` (default `false`) publishes renew events with the new expiry time, which saves every subscriber a Redis read per renewal. 5.x clients reject that payload: enable it only after all clients run 6.0.
</doc>

<doc title="Configuration Properties" path="guide/properties.md">
# Configuration Properties

Durations accept Spring Boot's formats (`10s`, `1m`, `PT10S`). Properties that control which config to load must be set in `bootstrap.yaml`.

## Common

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.cloud.cosky.enabled` | `true` | Enables CoSky (configuration and discovery). |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.namespace` | `cosky-{default}` | Namespace of the application's config and registration. A value without `{…}` is wrapped in a hash tag: `dev` becomes `{dev}`. |
| `spring.data.redis.*` | Spring Boot defaults | Redis connection (`url`, `host`, `port`, `password`, `cluster.nodes`, …), shared with the application. |

## Configuration

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.cloud.cosky.config.enabled` | `true` | Enables the config starter. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.config.config-id` | `${spring.application.name}.${file-extension}` | Config to load. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.config.file-extension` | `yaml` | Format of a config id without extension: `yaml`, `yml`, `properties` or `xml`. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.config.timeout` | `2s` | Maximum wait for the config at startup. |

## Service discovery

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.enabled` | `true` | Enables discovery and registration. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.order` | `0` | Order of CoSky's `DiscoveryClient` among several. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.timeout` | `2s` | Maximum wait of a blocking `DiscoveryClient` call. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.topology-enabled` | `true` | Records the application as a consumer of the services it discovers. |
| `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.filter-only-up-instances` | `true` | Returns only instances whose `instance_status` is `UP` or absent. |
| `spring.cloud.service-registry.auto-registration.enabled` | `true` | Registers the application at startup (Spring Cloud). |

### Registration

Prefix: `spring.cloud.cosky.discovery.registry`.

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `service-id` | `spring.application.name` | Service the instance belongs to. |
| `host` | first non-loopback IP | Address other services call. |
| `port` | web server port | Port other services call. |
| `schema` | `http` | URI scheme. |
| `weight` | `1` | Relative weight, used by CoSky's load balancers and Spring Cloud LoadBalancer's weighted configuration. |
| `is-ephemeral` | `true` | `true`: expires unless renewed. `false`: fixed, never expires. |
| `ttl` | `60s` | Lifetime of an ephemeral instance without renewal. |
| `renew.initial-delay` | `1s` | Delay before the first renewal. |
| `renew.period` | `10s` | Renewal interval; keep it well below `ttl`. |
| `metadata.<key>` | — | Metadata registered with the instance. |
| `initial-status` | `UP` | Value of the `instance_status` metadata at registration. |
| `timeout` | `2s` | Maximum wait for registration, deregistration and status changes. |
| `renew-event-carries-ttl-at` | `false` | Publishes renewals with the new expiry time, saving consumers a Redis read. Enable only once every client runs 6.0 or later. |

## REST API server

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.security.key` | — (required) | JWT signing secret; environment variable `COSKY_SECURITY_KEY`. |
| `cosky.security.enabled` | `true` | Enables authentication and authorization. |
| `cosky.security.enforce-init-super-user` | `false` | Resets the super user's password at every start; environment variable `COSKY_SUPER_INIT`. |
| `cosky.security.audit-log.action` | `write` | Requests to record: `read`, `write` or `rw`. |
| `cosky.security.audit-log.max-size` | `100000` | Newest audit entries kept. |
| `cosec.jwt.token-validity.access` | `15m` | Access token lifetime. |
| `cosec.jwt.token-validity.refresh` | `3H` | Refresh token lifetime. |
| `cosky.namespace` | `cosky-{system}` | Namespace of the server's own config and registration; environment variable `COSKY_NAMESPACE`. |
| `cosky.auto-registry` | `true` | Registers the server as service `cosky-rest-api`; environment variable `COSKY_AUTO_REGISTRY`. |
| `server.port` | `8080` | HTTP port. |

The server is a Spring Boot application: standard Spring Boot properties (logging, actuator, Redis) apply as well.
</doc>

<doc title="REST API" path="guide/rest-api.md">
# REST API

The REST API server exposes everything the dashboard does. The machine-readable contract is served by the server itself: OpenAPI at `/v3/api-docs` and Swagger UI at `/swagger-ui.html`.

## Conventions

- **Authentication**: sign in with `POST /v1/authenticate/{username}/login` and send `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>` on every other request. See [Security](./security.md#tokens).
- **Authorization**: requests on `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/…` need a role granting the namespace; user, role, namespace and audit endpoints need the `admin` role.
- **Namespaces** in paths are the full names, e.g. `{dev}` (URL-encoded: `%7Bdev%7D`). Instance ids contain `@` and `#`: URL-encode them too.
- **Errors** return `{"code": "0001", "msg": "<reason>"}` with status 400 for invalid requests, 401 without a valid token, 403 when not permitted, 404 for unknown routes.

## Authentication

| Method | Path | Body | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| POST | `/v1/authenticate/{username}/login` | `{"password": "…"}` | `{"accessToken", "refreshToken"}` |
| POST | `/v1/authenticate/{username}/refresh` | `{"accessToken", "refreshToken"}` | a new token pair |

## Namespaces

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces` | Namespaces you can access (all of them for administrators) |
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/current` | The server's own namespace |
| PUT | `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}` | Add a namespace |
| DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}` | Remove a namespace from the list |

## Configs

Prefix: `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/configs`.

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| GET | *(prefix)* | Config ids of the namespace |
| GET | `/{configId}` | Current config: `configId`, `data`, `hash`, `version`, `createTime` |
| PUT | `/{configId}` | Save (body: the raw content, `text/plain`); creates a version |
| DELETE | `/{configId}` | Remove |
| GET | `/{configId}/versions` | Versions in the history |
| GET | `/{configId}/versions/{version}` | Content of a version |
| PUT | `/{configId}/to/{targetVersion}` | Roll back to a version |
| GET | `/export` | All configs as a zip |
| POST | *(prefix)* `?policy=skip\|overwrite` | Import a zip (multipart field `importZip`); returns `{"total", "succeeded"}` |

## Services and instances

Prefix: `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/services`.

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| GET | *(prefix)* | Service ids |
| PUT | `/{serviceId}` | Add a service without instances |
| DELETE | `/{serviceId}` | Remove a service and its instance index |
| GET | `/{serviceId}/instances` | Live instances |
| PUT | `/{serviceId}/instances` | Register an instance (body below) |
| DELETE | `/{serviceId}/instances/{instanceId}` | Deregister an instance |
| PUT | `/{serviceId}/instances/{instanceId}/metadata` | Replace an instance's metadata (body: a string map) |
| GET | `/{serviceId}/lb` | One instance chosen by weighted random |
| GET | `/stats` | Instance count per service |

Registering an instance:

```json
{ "schema": "http", "host": "10.0.0.5", "port": 8080, "weight": 1, "isEphemeral": false, "metadata": { "zone": "a" } }
```

An ephemeral instance registered through the API expires after the TTL unless something renews it; register endpoints that cannot renew as fixed (`"isEphemeral": false`).

## Statistics

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/stat` | Counts of namespaces, configs, services (total and with instances) and instances |
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/stat/topology` | Consumers and the services they depend on |

Service statistics are refreshed every 10 seconds by one server instance, elected through Redis.

## Users, roles and audit

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/users` | Users with their roles and lock state |
| POST | `/v1/users/{username}` | Create (`{"password": "…"}`) |
| DELETE | `/v1/users/{username}` | Remove |
| PATCH | `/v1/users/{username}/password` | Change password (`{"oldPassword", "newPassword"}`) |
| PATCH | `/v1/users/{username}/role` | Replace roles (body: `["role", …]`) |
| PUT | `/v1/users/{username}/lock` | Lock |
| DELETE | `/v1/users/{username}/unlock` | Unlock |
| GET | `/v1/roles` | Roles |
| PUT | `/v1/roles/{roleName}` | Create or replace (`{"desc", "resourceActionBind": [{"namespace", "action": "r\|w\|rw"}]}`) |
| GET | `/v1/roles/{roleName}/bind` | Namespaces a role grants |
| DELETE | `/v1/roles/{roleName}` | Remove |
| GET | `/v1/audit-log?offset&limit&query&from&to&successful` | Audit entries, newest first; `from` / `to` in epoch milliseconds |
| GET | `/v1/audit-log/export?query&from&to&successful` | Matching entries as CSV |
</doc>

<doc title="Requirements" path="guide/requirements.md">
# Requirements

This page states what CoSky must do, with stable identifiers to reference in issues and pull requests. Every requirement names the tests that verify it, so a change that breaks one fails the build. New requirements are proposed through a feature request and added here with their tests.

## Scope

CoSky provides configuration management and service discovery for microservices, using only Redis as infrastructure. It is used as a library through Spring Cloud starters and the SDK, and optionally operated through the REST API server and its dashboard.

## Functional requirements

### Configuration

| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| FR-C1 | Configs are stored per namespace and config id, created, updated, read and removed. | `RedisConfigServiceTest`, `RestApiIntegrationTest.configLifecycle` |
| FR-C2 | Every change creates a new version; the latest 10 versions are kept and any of them can be rolled back to, including a removed config. | `RedisConfigServiceTest`, `RedisConsistencyConfigServiceTest.rollback` |
| FR-C3 | Applications receive config changes without polling, and a change made right after the first read is never lost. | `RedisConsistencyConfigServiceTest`, `CoSkyConfigRefresherTest` |
| FR-C4 | Spring Cloud applications load their config at startup, including multi-document YAML, and refresh on change. | `CoSkyPropertySourceLocatorTest`, `CoSkyConfigRefresherTest` |
| FR-C5 | Configs are exported to and imported from zip archives, skipping or overwriting existing configs, within size limits. | `ConfigControllerImportTest`, `ZipsTest`, `RestApiIntegrationTest.configLifecycle` |

### Service discovery

| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| FR-D1 | Instances register as ephemeral (kept alive by renewal) or fixed, and deregister. | `RedisServiceRegistryTest`, `RenewInstanceServiceTest` |
| FR-D2 | An ephemeral instance that stops renewing expires, is removed and announced, independently of the REST API server. | `InstanceExpiryReaperTest`, `RenewInstanceServiceRobustnessTest` |
| FR-D3 | An instance re-registered after expiring keeps the metadata set since its registration. | `RedisServiceRegistryTest.reRegisterAfterExpiryKeepsMetadataSetSince` |
| FR-D4 | Instance metadata can be set per key or replaced as a whole. | `RedisServiceRegistryTest` |
| FR-D5 | Clients discover services and their live instances, kept up to date by change events, never serving expired instances. | `ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscoveryTest`, `ConsistencyRenewEventTest` |
| FR-D6 | Load balancers choose among live instances (random and weighted), consistent with the discovery cache. | `RandomLoadBalancerTest`, `ArrayChooserTest`, `BinaryChooserTest`, `TreeChooserTest`, `LoadBalancerConsistencyTest` |
| FR-D7 | Consumers are recorded as dependents of the services they discover (topology). | `ServiceTopologyTest`, `TopologyRecordingServiceDiscoveryTest` |
| FR-D8 | Spring Cloud applications register themselves and discover others through the standard `DiscoveryClient` APIs. | `CoSkyDiscoveryClientTest`, `CoSkyServiceRegistryTest`, `CoSkyAutoServiceRegistrationAutoConfigurationTest` |
| FR-D9 | Spring Cloud clients receive only instances that are `UP` (or have no status), and see each instance's weight. | `CoSkyDiscoveryClientTest` |

### REST API server and security

| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| FR-S1 | Users authenticate with a password and receive JWT access and refresh tokens; anonymous requests to protected endpoints are rejected. | `RestApiIntegrationTest`, `RefreshTokenAuthenticationTest` |
| FR-S2 | Passwords are stored as BCrypt hashes; hashes of older versions are verified and upgraded on login. | `UserPasswordTest` |
| FR-S3 | Users are locked after repeated failed logins or by an administrator, and unlocked by an administrator. | `UserServiceTest`, `RestApiIntegrationTest.usersAndAuditLog` |
| FR-S4 | Roles grant read or read-write access per namespace; a user only sees and reaches the namespaces their roles grant. | `RbacServiceTest`, `RestApiIntegrationTest.namespaceRoleGrantsOnlyItsNamespace` |
| FR-S5 | The security policy can be replaced at runtime; an invalid policy never replaces a valid one. | `CoSkyPolicyTest` |
| FR-S6 | Operations are recorded in an audit log that can be filtered and exported. | `AuditLogServiceTest`, `AuditLogFilterTest`, `RestApiIntegrationTest.usersAndAuditLog` |

## Non-functional requirements

| ID | Requirement | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| NFR-1 | **Performance**: cached config and discovery reads are served from local memory, without a Redis round trip. | JMH benchmarks in CI, see [Performance](./performance.md) |
| NFR-2 | **Consistency**: every Redis mutation is a single Lua script, so concurrent writers never observe partial state. | `DiscoveryLuaKeysTest`, `ConfigLuaKeysTest`, `LuaScriptsTest` |
| NFR-3 | **Resilience**: a transient Redis failure is retried and never cached; the last good value keeps being served. | `ReactiveWatchCacheTest`, `RedisConsistencyConfigServiceErrorTest`, `ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscoveryErrorTest` |
| NFR-4 | **Bounded storage**: config history and the audit log are trimmed to fixed sizes. | `RedisConfigServiceTest.historyIsTrimmedToHistorySize`, `AuditLogRetentionTest` |
| NFR-5 | **Security by default**: the server refuses to start without a JWT secret, and users get no namespace access unless granted. | `JwtSecretValidatorTest`, `RestApiIntegrationTest` |
| NFR-6 | **Compatibility**: plain Redis, standalone or cluster (a namespace must carry a hash tag), with no Redis Functions or modules; Java 17+. | Integration tests against Redis in CI, [Architecture](./architecture.md#data-model) |
| NFR-7 | **Quality gates**: every change passes static analysis, license checks and at least 90% line / 70% branch coverage. | `./gradlew check` in CI, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) |
</doc>

<doc title="Architecture" path="guide/architecture.md">
# Architecture

This page explains how CoSky works, for engineers evaluating it, operating it at scale, or contributing to it.

## Principles

1. **Redis is the only infrastructure.** Clients talk to Redis directly; no CoSky server sits on the read or write path of applications.
2. **Every mutation is one Lua script**, so concurrent writers never see partial state, and every mutation announces itself on a Pub/Sub channel.
3. **Applications read from memory.** A local cache follows the change events, so reads cost no round trip and Redis load does not grow with read traffic.

## Modules

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#2d333b','primaryBorderColor':'#6d5dfc','primaryTextColor':'#e6edf3','lineColor':'#8b949e','secondaryColor':'#161b22','tertiaryColor':'#161b22'}}}%%
graph BT
    CORE["cosky-core"]
    CONFIG["cosky-config"] --> CORE
    DISCOVERY["cosky-discovery"] --> CORE
    SCC["cosky-spring-cloud-core"] --> CORE
    SCONFIG["cosky-spring-cloud-starter-config"] --> CONFIG
    SCONFIG --> SCC
    SDISC["cosky-spring-cloud-starter-discovery"] --> DISCOVERY
    SDISC --> SCC
    REST["cosky-rest-api"] --> SCONFIG
    REST --> SDISC
    style CORE fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style CONFIG fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style DISCOVERY fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style SCC fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style SCONFIG fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style SDISC fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    style REST fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
```

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `cosky-core` | Namespaces, Redis key helpers, the Lua script loader, event listener containers, and `ReactiveWatchCache`, the consistency cache everything else builds on |
| `cosky-config` | Config storage, versions and rollback (`RedisConfigService`), and its cached view (`RedisConsistencyConfigService`) |
| `cosky-discovery` | Registry, renewal and expiry, discovery and its cached view, load balancers, statistics, topology |
| `cosky-spring-cloud-*` | Spring Boot auto-configuration, Spring Cloud property source, `DiscoveryClient` and service registry |
| `cosky-rest-api` | REST API server and dashboard host: CoSec security, audit log, statistics job |

## Data model

Every key starts with its namespace. Namespaces are wrapped in a Redis Cluster hash tag (`{dev}`), so all keys of a namespace map to one slot and a Lua script can touch several of them.

| Key | Type | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `{ns}:cfg:{configId}` | hash | Current config: `data`, `hash`, `version`, `createTime` |
| `{ns}:cfg_idx` | set | Config ids |
| `{ns}:cfg_htr:{configId}:{version}` | hash | A previous version, with the operation that replaced it |
| `{ns}:cfg_htr_idx:{configId}` | sorted set | History keys by version; the latest 10 are kept |
| `{ns}:svc_idx` | set | Service ids |
| `{ns}:svc_itc_idx:{serviceId}` | set | Instance ids of a service |
| `{ns}:svc_itc:{instanceId}` | hash | Instance fields and metadata; a Redis TTL makes ephemeral instances expire |
| `{ns}:svc_itc_exp` | sorted set | Ephemeral instances by expiry time, to find expired ones without scanning |
| `{ns}:svc_stat` | hash | Instance count per service |
| `{ns}:topology_idx`, `{ns}:topology:{consumer}` | sets | Consumers, and the services each consumes |
| `cosky-{system}:ns_idx` | set | Namespaces listed in the dashboard |
| `cosky-{system}:…` | | Users, roles, login locks and the audit log of the REST API server |

Instance ids are `<serviceId>@<scheme>#<host>#<port>`. Instance metadata keys are stored with a `_` prefix; `__` marks internal fields.

## Writes and events

Each mutation runs as one Lua script and publishes on the channel named after the key it changed:

| Channel | Messages |
|---|---|
| `{ns}:cfg:{configId}` | `set`, `remove`, `rollback` |
| `{ns}:svc_idx` | `set`, `remove` (a service appeared or disappeared) |
| `{ns}:svc_itc:{instanceId}` | `register`, `deregister`, `expired`, `set_metadata`, `renew` (or `renew:<ttlAt>`) |
| `cosky-{system}:role_resource_bind:{role}` | `save`, `remove` |

Scripts share functions through `-- @include` directives resolved when they are loaded, and receive the keys they touch through `KEYS`, so they work unchanged on Redis Cluster and need no Redis Functions or modules.

## Consistency model

Every cached view (configs, services, instances, the security policy, roles) is a `ReactiveWatchCache`. For each key it:

1. **subscribes** to the key's channel and waits until the subscription is active,
2. **loads** the value from Redis, so no change can slip in between,
3. **applies** events one at a time, in order, publishing a new immutable snapshot only when the value actually changes.

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#2d333b','primaryBorderColor':'#6d5dfc','primaryTextColor':'#e6edf3','lineColor':'#8b949e','secondaryColor':'#161b22','tertiaryColor':'#161b22'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Writer
    participant R as Redis
    participant C as Cache (each application)
    C->>R: SUBSCRIBE channel
    C->>R: load value
    R-->>C: value (snapshot v1)
    W->>R: EVALSHA script (mutation + PUBLISH)
    R-->>C: event
    C->>R: reload or apply the change
    R-->>C: new value (snapshot v2)
```

Guarantees and limits:

- **Reads are eventually consistent**, typically within milliseconds of a write. A write is visible in Redis immediately; caches follow.
- **Lost messages heal.** Pub/Sub delivers at most once; every cached key is also reloaded every 5 minutes, which bounds the staleness after a missed message.
- **Failures are not cached.** A failed load is retried with backoff (1 s up to 30 s). Meanwhile the last good snapshot keeps being served; only a key that never loaded fails its readers.
- **Snapshots are shared.** A snapshot is prepared once per change and an unchanged value is the very same object, so readers can cache what they derive from it; load balancers reuse their state this way.
- **Cached keys stay.** A key, once read, keeps its subscription for the lifetime of the cache.

## Service discovery

**Expiry.** An ephemeral instance's hash has a Redis TTL, renewed by its client (every 10 s for a 60 s TTL by default). When Redis drops it, nothing would be announced, so each renewal also records the expiry time in `{ns}:svc_itc_exp`. After every renewal round, each client reaps up to 100 instances of its namespaces whose expiry time has passed: if the key is really gone, it removes the instance from its service and publishes `expired`. Reads perform the same cleanup lazily. No server is needed for instances to disappear.

**Renewal events are throttled.** A renewal is published only when the previously published expiry time is about to pass, so a stable fleet produces few events. By default consumers then re-read the instance's TTL; with `renew-event-carries-ttl-at`, the event carries the new expiry time instead (enable it only once every client runs 6.0).

**Expired instances are filtered on read** by comparing their expiry time with the local clock, so consumers do not depend on reaping latency. Keep clocks synchronized (NTP): a client whose clock runs ahead may treat live instances as expired.

## REST API server

The server is a Spring Boot application using the same starters as any application, plus:

- **CoSec** for JWT authentication and policy-based authorization ([Security](./security.md)),
- **Simba** to elect, through Redis, the one instance that refreshes service statistics every 10 seconds,
- **CosId** for distributed id generation.

It keeps no state of its own, so instances can be added and removed freely.

## Trade-offs

| Decision | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Redis as the only store | Nothing new to operate; Redis is fast and familiar | Redis availability and persistence become CoSky's; a Redis outage stops writes (cached reads continue) |
| Client renewal instead of server health checks | No server needed; scales with clients | A hung process that keeps renewing stays registered |
| Local caches fed by Pub/Sub | Reads in nanoseconds, Redis load independent of reads | Eventual consistency; one subscription per watched key |
| Lua scripts for every mutation | Atomicity without distributed locks | Scripts are part of the data contract; changing them needs care across client versions |
| Namespace hash tags | Cluster-safe multi-key scripts | A namespace cannot be spread over several cluster slots |
</doc>

<doc title="Performance" path="guide/performance.md">
# Performance

Applications read configs and instances from a **local cache**, so a read costs a map lookup instead of a Redis round trip. Writes and cache misses go to Redis and are bounded by its latency.

## Results

JMH throughput, 8 threads, against Redis on the same machine (Apple M4 Pro, JDK 17.0.20, Redis 8.10, JMH 1.37), measured on CoSky 6.0.0. Raw results: [`docs/jmh`](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/main/docs/jmh).

| Operation | Through | Throughput |
|---|---|---|
| Read a config | local cache (`RedisConsistencyConfigService`) | **706,727,232 ops/s** |
| Read a config | Redis (`RedisConfigService`) | 58,787 ops/s |
| Save a config | Redis | 20,498 ops/s |
| List services | local cache (`ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscovery`) | **771,907,860 ops/s** |
| List instances of a service | local cache | **64,012,445 ops/s** |
| List services | Redis (`RedisServiceDiscovery`) | 71,555 ops/s |
| List instances of a service | Redis | 9,818 ops/s |
| Register / renew / deregister an instance | Redis | 43,796 / 45,653 / 55,646 ops/s |

How to read these numbers:

- **Cached reads** scale with CPU cores; they are what applications pay on every config property access and every load-balanced call.
- **Redis operations** depend mostly on network latency and Redis itself. Over a real network expect fewer; on shared CI runners, roughly half.
- Each figure is a single 10-second measurement after a 10-second warm-up: use them for orders of magnitude and for comparing versions on the same machine, not as capacity guarantees.

## Why cached reads are cheap

A cached read returns an immutable snapshot prepared when the value last changed: no I/O, no lock, and for configs no allocation. Keeping the snapshot current costs one Redis Pub/Sub message per change, plus a reload of the changed key. [Architecture](./architecture.md#consistency-model) describes the mechanism.

## Reproducing

With Redis running on `localhost:6379`:

```bash
./gradlew :cosky-config:jmh :cosky-discovery:jmh -PjmhThreads=8
# one benchmark class
./gradlew :cosky-discovery:jmh -PjmhIncludes=ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscoveryBenchmark
```

Results are written to `<module>/build/results/jmh/results.json`. Options: `-PjmhThreads`, `-PjmhIncludes`, `-PjmhExcludes`, `-PjmhMode` (default `thrpt`).

The [benchmark workflow](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/.github/workflows/benchmark-test.yml) runs both suites on every push, which makes regressions visible between commits.
</doc>

<doc title="Internals" path="guide/internals.md">
# Internals

This page is for contributors. The process (setup, conventions, tests, pull requests, releases) is in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md); the design is in [Architecture](./architecture.md).

## Where things live

| To change… | Look at |
|---|---|
| The consistency cache | `cosky-core`: `cache/ReactiveWatchCache.kt` |
| Lua script loading and `-- @include` | `cosky-core`: `redis/LuaScripts.kt` |
| Config storage, versions | `cosky-config`: `redis/RedisConfigService.kt`, `src/main/resources/config_*.lua`, `cosky/config/config_lib.lua` |
| Registration, renewal, expiry | `cosky-discovery`: `redis/RedisServiceRegistry.kt`, `RenewInstanceService.kt`, `registry_*.lua`, `cosky/discovery/discovery_lib.lua` |
| Cached discovery | `cosky-discovery`: `redis/ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscovery.kt` |
| Redis key names | `ConfigKeyGenerator`, `DiscoveryKeyGenerator` (and the key functions of the Lua libraries) |
| Spring wiring and properties | `cosky-spring-cloud-*`: `*AutoConfiguration.kt`, `*Properties.kt` |
| REST endpoints | `cosky-rest-api`: `*Controller.kt`; paths in `support/RequestPathPrefix.kt` |
| Security | `cosky-rest-api`: `security/` and `src/main/resources/cosky-policy.json` |
| Dashboard | `dashboard/` (React; see its README) |
| Documentation | `wiki/` (VitePress; conventions in `wiki/AGENTS.md`) |

## Invariants and the tests that guard them

| Invariant | Guarded by |
|---|---|
| Every Redis mutation is one Lua script that publishes its change | Code review; `ConsistencyRedisServiceDiscoveryTest`, `RedisConsistencyConfigServiceTest` observe the events |
| Key names in Lua and in Kotlin agree | `ConfigLuaKeysTest`, `DiscoveryLuaKeysTest` |
| A cache subscribes before it loads, and applies events in order | `ReactiveWatchCacheTest` |
| A failed load is never cached | `ReactiveWatchCacheTest`, `*ErrorTest` |
| Expired instances are reaped without the server | `InstanceExpiryReaperTest` |
| The REST API enforces authentication and RBAC | `RestApiIntegrationTest` |

[Requirements](./requirements.md) maps every user-visible behavior to its tests.

## Changing the Redis data model

The key schema and the Lua scripts are a contract between client versions running side by side, so:

1. Add the key to the key generator **and** to the Lua library, and extend the matching `*LuaKeysTest`.
2. Pass every key a script touches through `KEYS` (needed for Redis Cluster), and publish on the changed key's channel.
3. Consider older clients: a new event payload or field must not break them, or must be opt-in (as `renew-event-carries-ttl-at` is).
4. Describe the change in [Architecture](./architecture.md#data-model) and, if it affects upgrades, in the upgrade guide.

## Tests

- Tests run against a real Redis on `localhost:6379`; extend `AbstractReactiveRedisTest` (module `cosky-test`) to get a template and clean-up.
- Use `me.ahoo.test.asserts.assert` for assertions and MockK for collaborators.
- `./gradlew check` also runs detekt, the license header check and the coverage floor.

## Debugging

```bash
redis-cli --scan --pattern '{dev}:*'              # keys of a namespace
redis-cli hgetall '{dev}:svc_itc:order-service@http#10.0.0.5#8080'
redis-cli psubscribe '{dev}:*'                    # watch every event of a namespace
redis-cli zrange '{dev}:svc_itc_exp' 0 -1 withscores   # ephemeral instances by expiry time
```

Raise `logging.level.me.ahoo.cosky` to `debug` to log cache loads, events and renewals.

## Benchmarks

JMH benchmarks live in `src/jmh` of `cosky-config` and `cosky-discovery`; see [Performance](./performance.md#reproducing). Compare before and after on the same machine when changing a hot path.
</doc>
